^1^ Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA. Correspondence: hossena@miamioh.edu

# Abstract

**Background.** The Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) has been
fielded nine times between 1993-94 and 2022 and underpins much of the
country's population and health evidence. Analyses of the respondent-level
data are, however, rarely checked against the officially published
estimates, and round-specific design features create traps that are easy to
miss.

**Methods.** We developed `bdhs`, an open-source R package that combines the
official estimates for all rounds with tools for the licensed microdata:
file identification, cross-round harmonization, complex survey designs, a
library of 97 indicators, fertility and mortality rates, data-quality
diagnostics, inequality and change analysis, and synthetic data calibrated
to the official estimates. Every indicator with a published value was
recomputed from the original recode files and compared with the official
figure.

**Results.** `r n_pass` of `r n_val` national comparisons across eight rounds
reproduced the official value (median absolute difference
`r fmt(stats::median(abs(val$computed - val$official)), 2)` percentage points). The validation exposed
analytic pitfalls with large effects: ignoring the 2022 short questionnaire
understates unmet need for family planning (`r fmt(pit$naive[1])`% vs
`r fmt(pit$correct[1])`%), treating the ever-married sample as all women
overstates child marriage by about ten points, and design effects of
`r fmt(min(deff$deff))` to `r fmt(max(deff$deff))` mean that analyses
ignoring the sampling design understate standard errors by up to
`r fmt(sqrt(max(deff$deff)))`-fold.

**Conclusions.** Validated, reproducible tooling removes avoidable error from
BDHS analyses and makes them easier to verify. Calibrated synthetic data allow
methods to be taught, tested and shared without access to the restricted
microdata.

**Keywords:** Demographic and Health Surveys; Bangladesh; survey methodology;
reproducibility; synthetic data; R

# Background

Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are the main source of nationally
representative data on fertility, family planning, maternal and child health
and nutrition in low- and middle-income countries. Bangladesh has conducted
nine DHS rounds (1993-94, 1996-97, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007, 2011, 2014,
2017-18 and 2022), implemented by the National Institute of Population
Research and Training (NIPORT) with ICF [@niport2024]. The official
estimates are published in final reports and through the DHS Program's
STATcompiler and API, while the respondent-level recode files are licensed
to registered researchers.

Secondary analyses of the BDHS are numerous, but their estimates are rarely
reconciled with the published figures. Doing so is harder than it seems. The
standard definitions in the *Guide to DHS Statistics* [@croft2018] interact
with round-specific design features: ever-married women's samples that
require all-woman factors, division boundaries and codes that changed three
times, a short women's questionnaire in 2022, and country-specific
questionnaire items. Errors in any of these steps propagate silently into
published results.

Existing tools address parts of the problem. `rdhs` provides access to the
DHS API and downloads datasets [@watson2019], `DHS.rates` computes
fertility and mortality rates [@dhsrates], `survey` implements design-based
estimation [@lumley2004], and IPUMS-DHS distributes harmonized extracts of
selected variables [@ipumsdhs]. None of them validates analyses of the
original files against the official estimates, documents the
country-specific pitfalls, or provides a way to share fully reproducible
analyses without the restricted data.

This paper describes `bdhs`, an R package for every BDHS round. It reports
(i) a systematic validation of 97 indicators against the official estimates;
(ii) the size of common analytic pitfalls; (iii) design effects; (iv) a
data-quality assessment across rounds; and (v) a method for synthetic BDHS
data calibrated to the official estimates. A case study of caesarean
delivery between 2004 and 2022 illustrates the change and inequality tools.

# Methods

## Data

`bdhs` bundles all `r format(310528, big.mark = ",")` official estimates
published for Bangladesh through the DHS Program API (all indicators, rounds
and breakdowns), the definitions of 2,607 indicators, catalogues of the
surveys and their 441 data files, cross-round codebooks (variable names and
labels only) and survey-specific division boundaries from the DHS Spatial
Data Repository. No respondent-level data are distributed. For the analyses
in this paper we used the author's licensed copies of the recode files: the
children's recode for 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007, 2011, 2014, 2017-18
and 2022; the births, household, women's and household-member recodes for
2017-18; and the women's and household-member recodes for 2022.

## Software design

The package reads DHS files identified by name or by content, harmonizes
112 variables across rounds with 1,008 round-specific rules (each checked
against the value labels in the data), and builds design objects with the
DHS sampling-error strata, clusters and normalized weights. Pooled analyses
keep each round's strata and clusters distinct and offer normalized,
de-normalized and equal weighting. Indicators are defined in code with their
denominator, reference period, weight and all-woman factor, so a single call
estimates any of them with design-based standard errors. Fertility and
childhood mortality rates use the DHS synthetic-cohort methods with
jackknife standard errors.

## Validation protocol

For every indicator with an official value we computed the national
estimate from each available recode file and compared it with the DHS
Program API value for the same reference period. A comparison passed when
the absolute difference was at most 0.5 percentage points (or the
equivalent for rates) plus half a unit of the official value's rounding.

## Pitfalls and design effects

For each analytic decision that changed results during validation, we
computed the estimate a naive analysis would give next to the correct
estimate. Design effects were computed as the ratio of the design-based
variance to the variance of a simple random sample of the same size.

## Data-quality diagnostics

`bdhs_quality()` implements standard DHS data-quality diagnostics
[@pullum2006]: age heaping in the household roster (Whipple index for ages
23-62 and Myers' blended index); age displacement at the boundaries of
eligibility for the women's interview (ratios of the number of women aged 50
to 49 and 14 to 15); completeness of birth dates; births by calendar year and
the ratio of births in the fifth to the fourth year before the survey, which
detects displacement of births out of the window for the health questions;
heaping of reported ages at death at 12 months; and anthropometric quality
(standard deviations of z-scores, flagged values and terminal-digit
preference in measured height). Statistics are unweighted, as in the DHS
data-quality tables.

## Calibrated synthetic data

```{r, results = "asis"}
if (is.null(syn)) cat("*[To be completed: description of the calibration method.]*")
```

## Change and inequality analysis

Changes between rounds are tested as differences of independent survey
estimates, with standard errors combined in quadrature; changes per year use
the midpoints of fieldwork. Within a round, contrasts between groups use the
full design-based covariance matrix. Wealth-related inequality is summarised
by the rich-poor difference and ratio, the slope and relative indices of
inequality (SII, RII) estimated by design-based regression on the weighted
ridit of wealth quintiles [@barros2013], the concentration index
[@wagstaff1991; @kakwani1997] and, for binary outcomes, Erreygers' corrected
concentration index [@erreygers2009]. Changes between two rounds are split
into a composition effect (changes in the distribution of a background
characteristic) and a within-group effect, using Kitagawa's symmetric
decomposition [@kitagawa1955; @dasgupta1993] with delete-one-cluster
jackknife standard errors. Progress towards the Sustainable Development
Goals is assessed from the official estimates as the average annual rate of
change since 2014 compared with the rate required to reach the 2030 target.

# Results

## Validation against official estimates

`r n_pass` of `r n_val` comparisons passed (Table 1). The median absolute
difference was below 0.04 percentage points in every round. The two
comparisons that did not pass concern women's anthropometry in 2022, which
the DHS Program computes from the household-member recode covering all women
in the biomarker subsample; the same indicators computed from that recode
reproduce the official values.

```{r}
if (!is.null(vbr)) {
  knitr::kable(vbr, col.names = c("Survey", "Recodes", "Comparisons", "Passed",
                                  "Median |difference|", "Max |difference| (passed)"),
               caption = "Table 1. Validation of computed national estimates against the official values.")
}
```

## Analytic pitfalls

Table 2 shows the size of each pitfall. The largest arise from the sampling
frame: treating the ever-married sample as all women overstates child
marriage by about ten percentage points, and ignoring the 2022 short
questionnaire understates unmet need by a third.

```{r}
if (!is.null(pit)) {
  knitr::kable(pit[, c("pitfall", "survey_id", "group", "naive", "correct", "official")],
               col.names = c("Pitfall", "Survey", "Group", "Naive", "Correct", "Official"),
               caption = "Table 2. Estimates from naive and correct analyses, with the official values.")
}
```

## Design effects

```{r}
if (!is.null(deff)) {
  knitr::kable(deff, col.names = c("Survey", "Indicator", "Estimate", "SE (design)",
                                   "SE (SRS)", "Design effect", "n"),
               caption = "Table 3. Design effects of headline indicators.")
}
```

## Data quality

Reporting of birth dates was essentially complete in every round
(`r fmt(min(qual$pct_birth_dates_complete, na.rm = TRUE))`-100% of births in
the children's recode had month and year). Anthropometric quality improved
markedly: the share of flagged height-for-age z-scores fell from
`r fmt(qual$child_haz_pct_flagged[qual$survey_id == "BD2007DHS"])`% in 2007 to
`r fmt(qual$child_haz_pct_flagged[qual$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"])`% in 2022, and
the share of child heights ending in 0 or 5 fell from
`r fmt(qual$child_height_pct_digit_0_or_5[qual$survey_id == "BD2000DHS"])`% in
1999-2000 to `r fmt(qual$child_height_pct_digit_0_or_5[qual$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"])`%
in 2022 (20% expected without preference). The standard deviation of
height-for-age z-scores nevertheless exceeded the WHO plausible range
(1.0-1.2) in every round with data. Age reporting in the household roster
was much less precise for men than for women (Whipple index
`r fmt(qual$whipple_men[qual$survey_id == "BD2017DHS"], 0)` vs
`r fmt(qual$whipple_women[qual$survey_id == "BD2017DHS"], 0)` in 2017-18), and
there were far fewer women recorded at age 50 than at 49 (ratio
`r fmt(qual$women_ratio_50_to_49[qual$survey_id == "BD2017DHS"], 2)` in 2017-18 and
`r fmt(qual$women_ratio_50_to_49[qual$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"], 2)` in 2022), a
pattern consistent with ages being shifted at the upper boundary of
eligibility. Reported ages at death were heaped at 12 months (heaping index
`r fmt(qual$heaping_12_months[qual$survey_id == "BD2017DHS"], 0)` in 2017-18,
where 100 means no heaping), which moves deaths between the infant and
child mortality intervals. We found no evidence of births being displaced
out of the five-year window in 2017-18 or 2022.

```{r}
qt <- qual
names(qt) <- c("Survey", "Birth dates complete (%)", "HAZ SD", "HAZ flagged (%)",
               "Height ending 0/5 (%)", "Whipple, men", "Whipple, women",
               "Women 50:49", "Heaping at 12 months")
knitr::kable(qt, digits = 2, caption = "Table 4. Data-quality indicators by round (unweighted).")
```

## Synthetic data fidelity

```{r, results = "asis"}
if (is.null(syn)) {
  cat("*[Synthetic-data results pending.]*")
} else {
  knitr::kable(syn, digits = 2, caption = "Table 5. Fidelity of calibrated synthetic data to the official estimates.")
}
```

## Case study: caesarean delivery, 2004-2022

Caesarean delivery rose from `r fmt(cs$estimate[cs$survey_id == "BD2000DHS"])`% of
births in 1999-2000 to `r fmt(cs$estimate[cs$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"])`% in 2022
(Figure 1), and every change between consecutive rounds was statistically
significant. Between 2004 and 2022 the increase was
`r fmt(cs_chg$difference[cs_chg$indicator == "rh_del_csection" & cs_chg$survey_1 == "BD2004DHS" & cs_chg$survey_2 == "BD2022DHS"])`
percentage points (`r fmt(cs_chg$annual_change[cs_chg$indicator == "rh_del_csection" & cs_chg$survey_1 == "BD2004DHS" & cs_chg$survey_2 == "BD2022DHS"], 2)` points
per year), faster than the rise in facility delivery relative to its level:
by 2022, `r fmt(100 * cs$estimate[cs$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"] / fd$estimate[fd$survey_id == "BD2022DHS"], 0)`%
of facility births were caesarean.

```{r fig1, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Caesarean and facility delivery, births in the three years before each survey (95% confidence intervals)."}
library(ggplot2)
yr <- c(BD2000DHS = 2000, BD2004DHS = 2004, BD2007DHS = 2007, BD2011DHS = 2011,
        BD2014DHS = 2014, BD2017DHS = 2018, BD2022DHS = 2022)
d <- cs_trend
d$year <- yr[d$survey_id]
d$what <- ifelse(d$indicator == "rh_del_csection", "Caesarean delivery", "Facility delivery")
ggplot(d, aes(year, estimate, colour = what)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percent of births", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Absolute inequality by household wealth widened as coverage expanded: the
slope index of inequality rose from `r fmt(iq("BD2004DHS", "sii"))` percentage points in
2004 to `r fmt(iq("BD2017DHS", "sii"))` in 2017-18 and was
`r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii"))` (95% CI `r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii", "ci_low"))`-`r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii", "ci_high"))`)
in 2022, while relative inequality fell steeply (RII from
`r fmt(iq("BD2004DHS", "rii"), 0)` to `r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "rii"))`) as the poorest
quintile began to use caesarean delivery (Table 6). Every measure computed from
the microdata agreed with the same measure computed from the official
quintile estimates (for example, Erreygers' index in 2022
`r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "eci"), 3)` vs `r fmt(iq("BD2022DHS", "eci", "official"), 3)`).

```{r}
tab <- cs_ineq[cs_ineq$measure %in% c("difference", "sii", "rii", "eci"), ]
tab <- reshape(tab[, c("survey_id", "measure", "estimate")], idvar = "survey_id",
               timevar = "measure", direction = "wide")
names(tab) <- c("Survey", "Rich-poor difference", "Erreygers CI", "RII", "SII")
knitr::kable(tab[, c("Survey", "Rich-poor difference", "SII", "RII", "Erreygers CI")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE, caption = "Table 6. Wealth-related inequality in caesarean delivery.")
```

Changes in the composition of mothers explained little of the increase.
Rising maternal education accounted for `r fmt(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "composition"))`
of the `r fmt(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "total"))` percentage-point increase between 2004 and 2022
(`r fmt(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "composition", "percent"), 0)`%), and changes in the
wealth distribution essentially none
(`r fmt(dc("BD2004DHS", "wealth_quintile", "composition", "percent"), 0)`%); the remainder occurred
within education and wealth groups (Table 7).

```{r}
dt <- cs_dec
dt$period <- paste(sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", dt$from), sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", dt$to), sep = "-")
dt$by <- ifelse(dt$by == "mother_edu_level", "Education", "Wealth quintile")
knitr::kable(dt[, c("period", "by", "component", "estimate", "se", "percent")], digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Period", "By", "Component", "Percentage points", "SE", "% of change"),
             caption = "Table 7. Kitagawa decomposition of the change in caesarean delivery.")
```

## Progress towards the SDGs

```{r}
st <- sdg[, c("sdg", "name", "baseline_value", "latest_value", "target", "aarc", "required_aarc", "on_track")]
knitr::kable(st, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("SDG", "Indicator", "2014", "2022", "Target", "AARC (%)", "Required AARC (%)", "On track"),
             caption = "Table 8. Progress towards SDG-related targets from the official estimates.")
```

Under-five mortality and stunting were on track for their 2030 targets,
whereas neonatal mortality, wasting and skilled birth attendance were not,
and child marriage, although declining, remained far from elimination
(Table 8).

# Discussion

Reproducing three decades of BDHS estimates from the recode files shows
that correct analysis is achievable but not automatic. With the survey
design, denominators, reference periods and round-specific rules encoded
once, `r n_pass` of `r n_val` national comparisons matched the official values,
typically to within a few hundredths of a percentage point, and inequality
measures computed from the microdata matched those derived from the official
quintile estimates. The same exercise exposed decisions that are invisible in
the data files but change results substantially.

The largest errors arise from the sampling frame rather than from
statistical method. Because every BDHS women's sample is restricted to
ever-married women, indicators of child marriage computed without all-woman
factors are about ten percentage points too high, which would make
Bangladesh's child-marriage problem appear considerably worse than it is.
Conversely, ignoring the short questionnaire introduced in 2022 understates
unmet need for family planning by a third, which would suggest a much faster
improvement since 2017-18 than actually occurred. Other pitfalls are smaller
but still exceed the sampling error: the treatment of births to very young
mothers in the general fertility rate, the inclusion of country-specific
feeding questions in exclusive breastfeeding, and the omission of the
measles-rubella vaccine. Several of these follow conventions that are
documented only implicitly in the published tables; for example, the
official child-marriage estimates by background characteristic use the total
all-woman factor rather than the subgroup factor recommended for other
all-women indicators.

Design effects between 1.6 and 3.1 for headline indicators mean that analyses
treating the BDHS as a simple random sample report confidence intervals up to
1.8 times too narrow, inflating the apparent precision of subgroup
comparisons. Comparisons across rounds raise a further, practical problem:
division codes were renumbered when Mymensingh division was created, so a
code that meant Rajshahi in 2014 means Mymensingh in 2017-18. Harmonized
division layouts, as provided by `bdhs`, are needed for any regional trend
analysis.

The data-quality diagnostics point to strengths and to issues worth keeping in
mind. Birth histories are complete, and there is no evidence of the
displacement of births out of the five-year window that affects mortality and
health indicators in some DHS countries. Anthropometric measurement improved
substantially after 2011. However, the dispersion of height-for-age z-scores
remains above the WHO plausible range, heaping of age at death at 12 months
shifts deaths between infant and child mortality, and a deficit of women
recorded at age 50 relative to 49 suggests age misreporting at the upper
boundary of eligibility. These patterns are consistent with earlier
assessments of age and date reporting in DHS surveys [@pullum2006].

The case study illustrates the analyses the package supports. Caesarean
delivery in Bangladesh rose about ten-fold between 2004 and 2022. Absolute
inequality by wealth widened as uptake spread from the richest households,
while relative inequality fell, and changes in maternal education and
household wealth explained only a small part of the increase. Most of the
rise occurred within every education and wealth group, consistent with
changes in health-system practice rather than in the characteristics of
mothers. Separating these components with appropriate standard errors is
straightforward once the design and the indicator definitions are correct.

`bdhs` complements rather than replaces existing tools. IPUMS-DHS
[@ipumsdhs] offers harmonized variables across countries, while `bdhs`
works directly on the original recode files of every BDHS round and validates
its results against the official estimates. `rdhs` [@watson2019] and
`DHS.rates` [@dhsrates] provide data access and demographic rates for all DHS
countries; `bdhs` reproduces the latter exactly and adds Bangladesh-specific
harmonization, validation and analysis tools.

This study has limitations. Validation was limited to the recode files
available to the author: children's recodes for most rounds, and complete
sets only for 2017-18 and 2022; no files from 1996-97 were available, so its
harmonization rules are marked as unverified. The validation tolerance of half
a percentage point does not guarantee agreement for subgroups, although
subgroup checks for selected indicators agreed closely. Model-based estimates
below the division level, which policy increasingly requires, are not
addressed.

# Conclusions

Analyses of the BDHS can reproduce the official estimates almost exactly, but
only when the sampling frame, questionnaire changes and country-specific
conventions are handled correctly; overlooking them changes key indicators by
up to ten percentage points. Encoding these rules in validated, open-source
software makes BDHS analyses more accurate, faster to conduct and easier to
verify. We recommend that analyses of DHS data report a validation against
the official national estimates alongside their results.

# Declarations

**Availability of data and materials.** The `bdhs` package is available at
<https://github.com/armanhossen-am/bdhs> under the MIT licence; the
analysis scripts and aggregate results are in its `paper/` folder. BDHS
microdata are available from The DHS Program to registered users
(<https://dhsprogram.com>).

**Ethics approval and consent to participate.** Secondary analysis of
de-identified survey data. The BDHS protocols were approved by the ICF
Institutional Review Board and the Bangladesh Medical Research Council, and
informed consent was obtained from all participants. Data access was granted
by The DHS Program.
